title: A Blood Test Can Now Screen You for Colon Cancer. The American Cancer Society Just Made It Official. South Asian Americans Have the Lowest Screening Rates in the Country.
excerpt: The Guardant Shield test detects tumour DNA in your blood. One in three eligible Americans remain unscreened. For South Asians, that number may be three in four.
body:
The American Cancer Society on Wednesday added a blood test to its official colorectal cancer screening recommendations for the first time, a decision that could reshape how millions of Americans — and particularly South Asian Americans, who have the lowest screening rates of any ethnic group — approach a disease that is increasingly striking younger adults.

The test is called Shield, made by the biotech company Guardant Health. It was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2024 and works by detecting fragments of tumour DNA circulating in the bloodstream. A simple blood draw at your doctor's office. No sedation, no preparation, no day off work.

## Why This Matters for South Asians

The numbers are stark. One in three eligible Americans has never been screened for colorectal cancer. Among South Asian Americans, community-based studies have found screening rates as low as 25 per cent — meaning three out of four people who should be tested are not.

A 2023 study published in the journal Cureus, analysing colon cancer rates among Asian Americans from 2017 to 2021, found rising incidence linked to socioeconomic factors, healthcare access gaps, and cultural barriers. A separate study from New York City's South Asian community, published in BMC Public Health, documented persistent disparities even after adjusting for insurance status and education.

The reasons are familiar to anyone who has navigated the Indian-American healthcare experience. Colonoscopy requires a full day of preparation, sedation, and recovery. It requires someone to drive you home. It requires explaining to your employer, your family, or yourself why you need to take a day for a procedure that feels abstract when you feel fine. For many first-generation immigrants, the cultural discomfort around discussing bowel health adds another layer of avoidance.

"We need to increase our emphasis on colorectal cancer as a highly preventable disease as much as a treatable one," said Dr Robert Smith, ACS vice president and senior author of the updated guideline.

## What the Blood Test Can and Cannot Do

Shield is not a replacement for colonoscopy. The ACS was explicit about this. Colonoscopy remains the gold standard — it allows doctors to both find and remove precancerous polyps in a single procedure.

The blood test is highly accurate at detecting advanced cancers but less sensitive at catching precancerous lesions and early-stage cancers. It is recommended specifically for people who decline or do not complete a colonoscopy or stool-based test.

The ACS also updated its recommended stool-based tests. The list now includes Exact Sciences' updated Cologuard and a new test called Colosense from Geneoscopy, both of which detect hidden blood and molecular markers.

The society's position is pragmatic: the most effective screening test is the one the patient actually completes.

## The Rising Threat in Younger Adults

Colorectal cancer is no longer a disease of the elderly. Cases among adults under 50 have been rising for two decades, and the ACS lowered its recommended screening age from 50 to 45 in 2018. The trend is particularly concerning for South Asian Americans, where dietary shifts after immigration — more processed food, less fibre, less fermented food — track with the same risk factors driving the increase.

A study of Asian American colorectal cancer mortality from 2018 to 2023, published in PubMed, highlighted ongoing disparities and called for disaggregated data to better understand subgroup-specific risks.

## What You Should Do

If you are 45 or older and have never been screened, the updated ACS guidelines give you three paths:

**Colonoscopy** remains the most thorough option. Every 10 years for average-risk individuals.

**Stool-based tests** — Cologuard or Colosense — can be done at home and mailed to a lab. They need to be repeated every three years.

**The Shield blood test** is for those who will not or cannot do the first two. It requires a blood draw and should be repeated every three years. A positive result still requires a follow-up colonoscopy.

The test is covered by most insurance plans, including Medicare, though coverage policies vary.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs whose parents live in India, the implications are different. India does not have a national colorectal cancer screening programme, and most adults over 45 have never been tested. If you are calling home this weekend, the conversation might be worth having. The disease is highly treatable when caught early — and increasingly deadly when it is not.

Most people who die from colorectal cancer had never been screened for it. That is the statistic the ACS is trying to change. For South Asian Americans, the gap is wider, the stakes are higher, and the excuses just got one fewer.
